{{Short description|Mathematical techniques used in probability theory and related fields}}{{Calculus}}

In [[probability theory]] and related fields, '''Malliavin calculus''' is a set of mathematical techniques and ideas that extend the mathematical field of [[calculus of variations]] from  deterministic functions to [[stochastic process]]es. In particular, it allows the computation of [[derivative]]s of [[random variable]]s. Malliavin calculus is also called the '''[[stochastic calculus]] of variations'''. P. Malliavin first initiated the calculus on infinite dimensional space. Then, significant contributors such as [[Seiichiro Kusuoka]], [[Daniel W. Stroock]], [[Jean-Michel Bismut]], [[Shinzo Watanabe]], [[Ichirō Shigekawa]], and so on completed the foundations for the field.

Malliavin calculus is named after [[Paul Malliavin]] whose ideas led to a [[mathematical proof|proof]] that [[Hörmander's condition]] implies the existence and smoothness of a [[probability density function|density]] for the solution of a [[stochastic differential equation]]; [[Lars Hörmander|Hörmander]]'s original proof was based on the theory of  [[partial differential equation]]s. The calculus has been applied to [[stochastic partial differential equation]]s as well.

The calculus allows [[integration by parts]] with random variables; this operation is used in [[mathematical finance]] to compute the sensitivities of [[derivative (finance)|financial derivative]]s. The calculus has applications in, for example, [[stochastic filtering]].

==Overview and history==
Malliavin introduced Malliavin calculus to provide a stochastic proof that [[Hörmander's condition]] implies the existence of a [[probability density function|density]] for the solution of a [[stochastic differential equation]]; [[Lars Hörmander|Hörmander]]'s original proof was based on the theory of  [[partial differential equation]]s. His calculus enabled Malliavin to prove regularity bounds for the solution's density. The calculus has been applied to [[stochastic partial differential equation]]s.

== Gaussian probability space ==
{{Main|Gaussian probability space}}
Consider a ''Wiener functional'' <math>F</math> (a functional from the [[classical Wiener space]]) and consider the task of finding a derivative for it. The natural idea would be to use the [[Gateaux derivative]]
:<math>D_g F[f] := \lim_{\tau \to 0} \frac{F[f + \tau g] - F[f]}{\tau}</math>,
however this does not always exist. Therefore it does make sense to find a new differential calculus for such spaces by limiting the directions.

The toy model of Malliavin calculus is an irreducible [[Gaussian probability space]] <math>X=(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P,\mathcal{H})</math>. This is a (complete) probability space <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)</math> together with a closed [[Space (mathematics)|subspace]] <math>\mathcal{H}\subset L^2(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)</math> such that all <math>H\in \mathcal{H}</math> are mean zero Gaussian variables and <math>\mathcal{F}=\sigma(H:H\in \mathcal{H})</math>. If one chooses a basis for <math>\mathcal{H}</math> then one calls <math>X</math> a ''numerical model''. On the other hand, for any separable Hilbert space <math>\mathcal{G}</math> exists a canonical irreducible Gaussian probability space <math>\operatorname{Seg}(\mathcal{G})</math> named the ''Segal model'' (named after [[Irving Segal]]) having <math>\mathcal{G}</math> as its Gaussian subspace. In this case for a <math>g\in \mathcal{G}</math> one notates the associated random variable in <math>\operatorname{Seg}(\mathcal{G})</math> as <math>W(g)</math>.

Properties of a Gaussian probability space that do not depend on the particular choice of basis are called ''intrinsic'' and such that do depend on the choice ''extrensic''.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Paul |last1=Malliavin| publisher=Springer|title=Stochastic Analysis|series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften|place=Berlin, Heidelberg|date=1997|isbn=3-540-57024-1|pages=4–15}}</ref> We denote the countably infinite product of real spaces as <math>\R^{\N}=\prod\limits_{i=1}^{\infty}\R</math>.

Recall the modern version of the [[Cameron–Martin_theorem#Version for locall convex vector spaces|Cameron-Martin theorem]]
: ''Consider a [[locally convex vector space]] <math>E</math> with a cylindrical Gaussian measure <math>\gamma</math> on it. For an element in the topological dual <math>f\in E'</math> define the distance to the mean''
::<math>t_{\gamma}(f):=f-\int_E f(x) \gamma(\mathrm{d}x),</math>
: ''which is a map <math>t_{\gamma}\colon E'\to L^2(E,\gamma)</math>, and denote the closure in <math>L^2(E,\gamma)</math> as''
::<math>E_{\gamma}':=\operatorname{clos}\left\{t_{\gamma}(f)\colon\ f\in E'\right\}</math>
: ''Let <math>\gamma_{m}:=\gamma(\cdot - m)</math> denote the translation by <math>m\in E</math>. Then <math>E_{\gamma}'</math> respectively the [[covariance operator]] <math>R_{\gamma}:E_{\gamma}'\to (E_{\gamma}')^*</math> on it induces a [[reproducing kernel Hilbert space]] <math>R</math> called the Cameron-Martin space such that for any <math>m\in R</math> there is [[Equivalence (measure theory)|equivalence]] <math>\gamma_{m}\sim \gamma</math>.''<ref>{{cite book |first1=Vladimir |last1=Bogachev| publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|title=Gaussian Measures|place=Rhode Island|date=1998}}</ref>
In fact one can use here the [[Feldman–Hájek theorem]] to find that for any other <math>h\not \in R</math> such measure would be singular.

Let <math>\gamma</math> be the canonical Gaussian measure, by transferring the Cameron-Martin theorem from <math>(\R^{\N},\mathcal{B}(\R^{\N}),\gamma^{\N}=\otimes_{n\in\N} \gamma)</math> into a numerical model <math>X</math>, the additive group of <math>\mathcal{H}</math> will define a quasi-automorphism group on <math>\Omega</math>. A construction can be done as follows: choose an orthonormal basis in <math>\mathcal{H}</math>, let <math>\tau_{\alpha}(x)=x+\alpha</math> denote the translation on <math>\R^\N</math> by <math>\alpha</math>, denote the map into the Cameron-Martin space by <math>j:\mathcal{H}\to \ell^2</math>, denote
:<math>L^{\infty-0}(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)=\bigcap\limits_{p<\infty}L^p(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)\quad</math> and <math>\quad q:L^{\infty-0}(\R^{\N},\mathcal{B}(\R^{\N}),\gamma^{\N})\to L^{\infty-0}(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P),</math>
we get a canonical representation of the additive group <math>\rho:\mathcal{H}\to \operatorname{End}(L^{\infty-0}(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P))</math> acting on the [[endomorphism]]s by defining
:<math>\rho(h)=q\circ \tau_{j(h)}\circ q^{-1}.</math>

One can show that the action of <math>\rho</math> is extrinsic meaning it does not depend on the choice of basis for <math>\mathcal{H}</math>, further <math>\rho(h+h')=\rho(h)\rho(h')</math>
for <math>h,h'\in \mathcal{H}</math> and for the [[C0-semigroup#Infinitesimal_generator|infinitesimal generator]] of <math>(\rho(h))_{h}</math> that
:<math>\lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0}\frac{\rho(\varepsilon h)-I}{\varepsilon}=M_h</math>
where <math>I</math> is the identity operator and <math>M_h</math> denotes the multiplication operator by the random variable  <math>h\in \mathcal{H}</math> (acting on the endomorphisms). In the case of an arbitrary Hilbert space <math>\mathcal{G}</math> and the Segal model <math>\operatorname{Seg}(\mathcal{G})</math> one has <math>j:\mathcal{G}\to \ell^2</math> (and thus <math>\rho:\mathcal{G}\to \operatorname{End}(L^{\infty-0}(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P))</math>. Then the limit above becomes the multiplication operator by the random variable <math>W(g)</math> associated to <math>g\in \mathcal{G}</math>.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Paul |last1=Malliavin| publisher=Springer|title=Stochastic Analysis|series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften|place=Berlin, Heidelberg|date=1997|isbn=3-540-57024-1|pages=20–22}}</ref>

For <math>F\in L^{\infty-0}(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)</math> and <math>h\in\mathcal{H}</math> one now defines the directional derivative
:<math>\langle DF,h\rangle=D_h F=\lim\limits_{\varepsilon \to 0}\frac{\left(\rho(\varepsilon h)-I\right)F}{\varepsilon}.</math>

Given a Hilbert space <math>H</math> and a Segal model <math>\operatorname{Seg}(H)</math> with its Gaussian space <math>\mathcal{H}=\{W(h): h\in H\}</math>. One can now deduce for <math>F\in L^{\infty-0}(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)</math> the integration by parts formula
:<math>\mathbb{E}[D_h F]=\mathbb{E}[M_{W(h)}F]=\mathbb{E}[W(h)F]</math>.<ref>{{cite book |first1=Paul |last1=Malliavin| publisher=Springer|title=Stochastic Analysis|series=Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften|place=Berlin, Heidelberg|date=1997|isbn=3-540-57024-1|pages=36}}</ref>

== Invariance principle ==
The usual invariance principle for [[Lebesgue integration]] over the whole real line is that, for any real number ε and integrable function ''f'', the
following holds

:<math> \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)\, d \lambda(x) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x+\varepsilon)\, d \lambda(x) </math> and hence <math>\int_{-\infty}^\infty f'(x)\, d \lambda(x)=0.</math>

This can be used to derive the [[integration by parts]] formula since, setting ''f'' = ''gh'', it implies

:<math>0 = \int_{-\infty}^\infty f' \,d \lambda = \int_{-\infty}^\infty (gh)' \,d \lambda = \int_{-\infty}^\infty g h'\, d \lambda +
\int_{-\infty}^\infty g' h\, d \lambda.</math>

A similar idea can be applied in stochastic analysis for the differentiation along a Cameron-Martin-Girsanov direction. Indeed, let <math>h_s</math> be a square-integrable [[predictable process]] and set

:<math> \varphi(t) = \int_0^t h_s\, d s .</math>

If <math>W</math> is a [[Wiener process]], the [[Girsanov theorem]] then yields the following analogue of the invariance principle:

:<math> E(F(W + \varepsilon\varphi))= E \left [ F(W) \exp \left ( \varepsilon\int_0^1 h_s\, d w_s -
\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^2 \int_0^1 h_s^2\, ds \right ) \right ].</math>

Differentiating with respect to ε on both sides and evaluating at ε=0, one obtains the following integration by parts formula:

:<math>E(\langle DF(W), \varphi\rangle) = E\Big[ F(W) \int_0^1 h_s\, dw_s \Big].
</math>

Here, the left-hand side is the [[Malliavin derivative]] of the random variable <math>F</math> in the direction <math>\varphi</math> and the integral appearing on the right hand side should be interpreted as an [[Itô integral]].

== Clark–Ocone formula ==
{{Main|Clark–Ocone theorem}}

One of the most useful results from Malliavin calculus is the [[Clark–Ocone theorem]], which allows the process in the [[martingale representation theorem]] to be identified explicitly. A simplified version of this theorem is as follows:

Consider the standard Wiener measure on the canonical space <math>C[0,1]</math>, equipped with its canonical filtration. For <math>F: C[0,1] \to \R</math> satisfying <math> E(F(X)^2) < \infty</math> which is Lipschitz and such that ''F'' has a strong derivative kernel, in the sense that
for <math>\varphi</math> in ''C''[0,1]

:<math> \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac 1 \varepsilon (F(X+\varepsilon \varphi) - F(X) ) = \int_0^1 F'(X,dt) \varphi(t)\ \mathrm{a.e.}\ X</math>

then

:<math>F(X) = E(F(X)) + \int_0^1 H_t \,d X_t ,</math>

where ''H'' is the previsible projection of ''F''<nowiki>'</nowiki>(''x'', (''t'',1]) which may be viewed as the derivative of the function ''F'' with respect to a suitable parallel shift of the process ''X'' over the portion (''t'',1] of its domain.

This may be more concisely expressed by

:<math>F(X) = E(F(X))+\int_0^1 E (D_t F \mid \mathcal{F}_t ) \, d X_t .</math>

Much of the work in the formal development of the Malliavin calculus involves extending this result to the largest possible class of functionals ''F'' by replacing the derivative kernel used above by the "[[Malliavin derivative]]" denoted <math>D_t</math> in the above statement of the result. {{Citation needed|date=August 2011}}

== Skorokhod integral ==
{{Main|Skorokhod integral}}
The [[Skorokhod integral]] operator, which is conventionally denoted δ, is defined as the adjoint of the Malliavin derivative in the [[white noise]] case when the Hilbert space is an <math>L^2</math> space; thus for ''u'' in the domain of the operator which is a subset of <math>L^2([0,\infty) \times \Omega)</math>,
for ''F'' in the domain of the Malliavin derivative, we require

: <math> E (\langle DF, u \rangle ) = E (F \delta (u) ),</math>

where the inner product is that on <math>L^2[0,\infty)</math>, viz.

: <math> \langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^\infty f(s) g(s) \, ds.</math>

The existence of this adjoint follows from the [[Riesz representation theorem]] for linear operators on [[Hilbert spaces]].

It can be shown that if ''u'' is adapted then

: <math> \delta(u) = \int_0^\infty u_t\, d W_t ,</math>

where the integral is to be understood in the Itô sense.  Thus this provides a method of extending the Itô integral to non-adapted integrands.

==Applications==
The calculus allows [[integration by parts]] with [[random variable]]s; this operation is used in [[mathematical finance]] to compute the [[Sensitivity analysis|sensitivities]] of [[derivative (finance)|financial derivative]]s. The calculus has applications for example in [[stochastic control|stochastic filtering]].
